message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"20.11","text":"Just as a meal was about to be served to us, someone slipped in and said, “Appion the Many-Victor has just arrived from Antioch with Annoubion and is staying as Simon’s guest.” When our father heard this, he rejoiced and said to Peter, “If you permit me, I will go greet Appion and Annoubion, who have been my friends from earliest youth. Perhaps I may persuade Annoubion to debate Clement about nativity.” Peter said, “I permit it, and I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship. But consider how, by God’s providence, everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony. I say this because Annoubion’s arrival has proved advantageous to you.” Our father replied, “I truly see that this is so.” After saying this, he went to Simon.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἀππίων ὁ πλειστονίκης","chosen":"Appion the Many-Victor","rationale":"πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet denoting numerous victories rather than silently transliterated as another personal name."},{"source_quote":"περὶ γενέσεως","chosen":"about nativity","rationale":"In this debate setting γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, particularly as a subject of astrological determinism; “birth” or “genesis” remains possible more generally."},{"source_quote":"ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη","chosen":"I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship","rationale":"The idiom describes performing the part or duties belonging to friends; the English avoids reproducing the awkward literal image of “parts.”"},{"source_quote":"πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν","chosen":"everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony","rationale":"οἰκείαν is taken with τὴν ἁρμονίαν as “fitting”; attachment to πληροφορίαν, yielding something like “your own assurance,” is also grammatically possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"20.12","text":"As for us who were with Peter, we spent the whole night asking questions one after another, remaining awake because of the pleasure and joy produced by what was being said. When the night was already beginning somehow to brighten, Peter looked at me and my brothers and said, “I am perplexed about what your father decided.” While he was saying this, our father arrived there and found Peter discussing him with us. Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained why he had slept outside. We stared at him in astonishment, seeing Simon’s appearance but hearing the voice of our father Faustus. As we recoiled from him and regarded him with loathing, our father was astounded at being treated so harshly and hostilely by us. Only Peter, who saw his natural form, said to us, “Why do you push your father away in disgust?” We and our mother replied, “To us this man looks like Simon, though he has our father’s voice.” Peter said, “For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes his appearance too is visible as it really is: he is not Simon but Faustus, your father.” Then, looking directly at our father too, he said, “......... appearance of yours is not visible to them, but Simon’s—the most impious man’s—is; and to us .........”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"νήφοντες ἐνυκτερεύσαμεν","chosen":"we spent the whole night ... remaining awake","rationale":"Here νήφω concerns wakeful alertness during the night rather than literal abstinence from intoxication; “remaining clear-minded” is a possible but less contextual rendering."},{"source_quote":"ἀθυμοῦντα ἰδὼν","chosen":"Seeing Peter disheartened","rationale":"The unexpressed object of ἰδών is taken as Peter, whom the arriving father has just found discussing him; attachment to another participant is less natural but not formally impossible."},{"source_quote":"τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν","chosen":"who saw his natural form","rationale":"κατὰ φύσιν identifies the form belonging to his real nature, in contrast to the magically imposed appearance."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ ... τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς","chosen":"his unbewitched voice ... my unbewitched eyes","rationale":"ἀμάγευτος is rendered directly as freedom from magical alteration or deception, preserving the repeated source term."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........","issue":"The selected edition prints two lacunae of nine dots each. After the first, only the isolated form or word-ending “όν” survives, so the missing modifier or construction cannot be recovered. Both nine-dot gaps remain explicit in the translation, and no restoration is supplied.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"20.13","text":"While Peter was saying this, one of the advance messengers came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “I want you to know, my lord, that Simon, by publicly performing many marvels in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, has stirred them to such hatred that every person among those staying there longs to taste your very flesh. Consequently, when we advance messengers and our brothers whom you had planted with Simon saw the city gnashing furiously against you, we met secretly in one place to consider what must be done. While we were at a loss, Cornelius arrived, a centurion sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed. We summoned him secretly, explained the reason for our discouragement, and appealed to him for help. He very eagerly promised to frighten Simon into flight. If only we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘With me keeping watch and secretly claiming through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him—because Caesar has executed many magicians, learned the facts about him, and sent me to seek him so that he might punish him just like the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report, as though they had secretly heard it somewhere, that I have been sent to arrest him. Perhaps when he hears it, he will take fright and flee.’ So, although we had considered doing something else, it nevertheless happened in this way. For after hearing the report both from many outsiders, who told him secretly in order to ingratiate themselves with him in important matters, and also from our agents inside, he received the information as though from his own people and decided to withdraw. He therefore escaped from Antioch and, as we have heard, came here with Athenodorus. We consequently advise you not yet to enter that city, until we know whether, with him absent, they will be able to recover from his slander against you.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τις τῶν προόδων","chosen":"one of the advance messengers","rationale":"πρόοδοι denotes people who go ahead or operate in advance; “forerunners” is possible but less clear in this organizational context."},{"source_quote":"πολλὰ τεράστια ποιῶν","chosen":"performing many marvels","rationale":"τεράστια denotes extraordinary portent-like feats; “wonders” or, with a hostile nuance, “monstrous feats” are alternatives."},{"source_quote":"μάγον σε ὀνομάζων καὶ γόητα","chosen":"calling you a magician and a sorcerer","rationale":"The two accusations are kept distinct. γόης can also mean “conjurer,” “charlatan,” or “impostor,” but the magical context supports “sorcerer.”"},{"source_quote":"σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου","chosen":"to taste your very flesh","rationale":"αὐτῶν is taken intensively with the plural σαρκῶν, heightening the violent image rather than referring to another group’s flesh."},{"source_quote":"ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος","chosen":"the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed","rationale":"The main rendering takes ὅν as referring back to Cornelius. Because the provincial governor is the nearer masculine antecedent, reference to the governor is grammatically possible and cannot be excluded solely from the sentence."},{"source_quote":"Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περισκοποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος","chosen":"With me keeping watch and secretly claiming through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him","rationale":"The genitive construction describes Cornelius maintaining surveillance while causing or allowing the claim to circulate through friends. The precise attachment of διὰ πολλῶν φίλων and κρύφα is flexible."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἔξω εἰς τὰ μεγάλα αὐτῷ χαριζομένων","chosen":"outsiders ... in order to ingratiate themselves with him in important matters","rationale":"The phrase describes outsiders seeking his favor in substantial or important affairs; “who did him great favors” is another viable rendering."},{"source_quote":"ὡς παρ’ ἰδίων γνώμην εἰληφὼς","chosen":"he received the information as though from his own people","rationale":"γνώμη here is understood as intelligence or information rather than merely an abstract opinion or judgment."},{"source_quote":"τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται","chosen":"with him absent, they will be able to recover from his slander against you","rationale":"The context calls for relief, cessation, or recovery from the effects of the slander. The unusual form ὑπολῆσαι makes the exact nuance uncertain."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας ........... λέγων Πέτρῳ","issue":"The selected edition prints an eleven-dot lacuna between “from Antioch” and “saying to Peter.” The missing wording is unavailable; the eleven dots are retained and no identity, description, or adverb is restored.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὑπολῆσαι","issue":"The selected reading is lexically unusual in this construction and may reflect loss of ξ from a form of ὑπολήγω, “abate” or “cease.” The translation follows the contextual sense while preserving the supplied reading in this note.","proposed_reading":"ὑπολῆξαι","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"20.14","text":"When the advance messenger had reported these things, Peter looked directly at our father and said, “Do you hear, Faustus? Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician, as is now evident. Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm, he fled in fear, placing his own form upon you so that, when you died, grief would come upon your children.” Hearing this, our father wept and lamented, saying, “You have judged correctly, Peter. Annoubion ...... of mine, because he loved me, cryptically disclosed the plot, and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν","chosen":"Your transformation was brought about","rationale":"The passive sense supplied by ὑπὸ Σίμωνος presents Simon as the agent responsible for Faustus’s altered appearance."},{"source_quote":"Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν","chosen":"Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm","rationale":"ἐπὶ κακῷ indicates harmful or punitive intent without specifying the precise punishment."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σοὶ περιθεὶς μορφήν","chosen":"placing his own form upon you","rationale":"The concrete image of wrapping or putting Simon’s appearance around Faustus is retained rather than reduced to simple resemblance."},{"source_quote":"μυστηριωδῶς τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ἐξέφηγε","chosen":"cryptically disclosed the plot","rationale":"μυστηριωδῶς indicates an indirect, mysterious, or cryptic disclosure; ἐπιβουλή is a hostile plot or design."},{"source_quote":"οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος","chosen":"I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer","rationale":"The first-person speaker and following first-person ἤμην support “I,” but the exact completion and object of the broken verb remain unavailable and are not restored."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Ἀννουβίων ...... μού με φιλῶν","issue":"The selected edition prints a six-dot lacuna before μού. The surviving “of mine” indicates a lost description or relationship, but its wording cannot be recovered. The six dots remain explicit.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος","issue":"The selected edition prints ten dots immediately after the surviving verbal stem ἐπίστευ-. The precise verbal ending and any following words are unavailable; the ten-dot gap is retained without supplying an object or other lost content.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"20.15","text":"After our father said this, not long afterward ....... to us, reporting Simon’s flight to us and that he had set out for Judea that very night. He found our father beating himself and saying with lamentation, “Alas, wretch that I am! Though I heard that he was a magician, miserable man that I am, I refused to believe it. After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day, I quickly returned to my former calamity of being unknown.” Our mother, lamenting, kept tearing out her hair, while we groaned in distress over our father’s alteration, unable to understand what on earth it was. When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood speechless. Before everyone, Peter said to us children, “Believe me: this is Faustus, your father. I therefore command you to pay him the regard due to a father, for God will provide some occasion through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again.” After saying this to us, he looked at our father and said, “I permitted you to greet Appion and Annoubion because you acknowledge that they have been your friends since childhood, not to associate with Simon the magician.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κοπτόμενον","chosen":"beating himself","rationale":"κόπτομαι can describe striking oneself as an embodied act of mourning; the accompanying lament supports retaining that concrete action."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις","chosen":"After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day","rationale":"ἐπιγινώσκω here concerns recognition of identity, while σύμβιος denotes one’s spouse or life-partner; the context identifies Faustus’s wife."},{"source_quote":"τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ... συμφοράν","chosen":"my former calamity of being unknown","rationale":"ἀγνοία is understood contextually as failure by his family to recognize him, not mere intellectual ignorance."},{"source_quote":"ἀχανὴς ἔστη","chosen":"he stood speechless","rationale":"ἀχανής depicts stunned, open-mouthed immobility; “stood dumbfounded” or “stood aghast” would also preserve the reaction."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πατρὶ προσέχειν","chosen":"to pay him the regard due to a father","rationale":"προσέχειν calls for attention, adherence, or care toward Faustus in his paternal identity; “attend to him as a father” is more literal but less idiomatic."},{"source_quote":"δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν","chosen":"through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again","rationale":"The subject of “stripping off” and “revealing” is taken contextually as Faustus, while “your father’s form” supplies in English the noun understood elliptically after τὴν τοῦ πατρός."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν","issue":"The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after “not long afterward.” The missing subject and finite expression governing “to us” are unavailable. The translation retains all seven dots and does not identify the arriving reporter.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
